segments.text: What if every single person on Earth jumped at exactly the same moment?
{8.3|Eight point three} billion people, all over the world, counting down together.
Three.
Two.
One.
Jump!
Would we shake the planet?
Trigger a huge earthquake?
Or even knock Earth out of its orbit?
Surprisingly, almost nothing happens.
We push down on Earth, and Earth pushes us back up.
So the planet does move, but it's over ten trillion times heavier than all of us.
Even if we all jumped from one spot, it would shift less than the width of an atom.
And spread around the globe, our pushes partly cancel out.
When everyone lands, there's plenty of noise, and tiny vibrations nearby.
But billions of small, scattered taps are nothing like one earthquake.
No planet-wide quake, no tsunami, and no change to Earth's orbit.
{8.3|Eight point three} billion people. One perfect jump.
And Earth barely notices.
That's how massive our planet really is.
So, what should we test next?
